stem: In an experiment, renal medullary interstitial osmolality is measured in an anesthetized animal at baseline.  Vasopressin is then infused intravenously, causing the medullary interstitial osmolality to rise and the urine to become progressively more concentrated.  The researchers find that the increase in interstitial osmolality is partly due to increased reabsorption of a solute other than sodium chloride.  Vasopressin acts at which of the following nephron segments to produce this effect?​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌

options.label: E
options.text: Thin descending limb of the loop of Henle

explanation:
Vasopressin, or antidiuretic hormone (ADH), promotes water retention by increasing collecting duct water permeability and helping maintain the medullary osmotic gradient.  Interstitial osmolality increases from the renal cortex toward the inner medulla, primarily due to sodium chloride and urea.  This gradient pulls water out of the collecting duct as it passes through the medulla, concentrating the urine.

ADH activates V2 receptors, resulting in insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane of collecting duct principal cells.  These channels increase water permeability, allowing water to move from the tubular fluid into the surrounding interstitium by osmosis.  Because the cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts have low urea permeability, urea largely remains in the tubular fluid as water is reabsorbed, progressively increasing the tubular urea concentration.

In the inner medullary collecting duct, ADH also increases the activity and membrane abundance of urea transporters (UT-A1 and UT-A3).  These transporters allow urea to diffuse passively down its concentration gradient from the tubular fluid into the medullary interstitium.  Some of this urea enters the thin limbs of the loop of Henle and flows through the nephron back to the collecting duct, a process called urea recycling.  This recycling helps retain urea within the inner medulla, reinforcing the osmotic gradient that drives water reabsorption and permits production of maximally concentrated urine.

(Choice A)  ADH increases water reabsorption in the cortical collecting duct through aquaporin-2 insertion, reducing water delivery to the medulla and helping preserve its osmotic gradient.  However, this segment has low urea permeability and is not the site of ADH-stimulated urea reabsorption.

(Choice B)  The early distal tubule reabsorbs sodium chloride but is relatively impermeable to water and urea.  It does not mediate ADH-stimulated urea reabsorption.

(Choice D)  The proximal tubule passively reabsorbs approximately half of the filtered urea as water reabsorption increases the tubular urea concentration.  This process is not regulated by ADH.

(Choice E)  Portions of the thin descending limb permit urea to enter the tubular lumen from the medullary interstitium, contributing to urea recycling.  This movement is opposite to the urea reabsorption described in the experiment, which occurs in the inner medullary collecting duct.

Educational objective:Antidiuretic hormone increases urea permeability in the inner medullary collecting duct, allowing urea to diffuse into the medullary interstitium.  Urea accumulation and recycling help maintain the medullary osmotic gradient, promoting water reabsorption and production of concentrated urine.​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌
